newsitem.title: NORWAY: Nobel group uses peace prize to sway world events.
newsitem.headline: Nobel group uses peace prize to sway world events.

text.p: Norway's Nobel Committee has once again used its power to swing a spotlight of world attention onto the protagonists of a lonely, often forgotten struggle.

In naming two East Timor figures -- Roman Catholic Bishop Carlos Belo and Jose Ramos-Horta, who leads an anti-Indonesian resistance movement from his base in Australia -- as winners of the Nobel Peace Prize, the committee was sure to offend the government in Jakarta.
The committee has often in the past angered governments by picking winners at odds with the authorities of their own homelands.

Indonesia, which already included West Timor, invaded the the eastern half of the island after Portugal abandoned its colonial rule there in 1975. Its annexation of the territory a year later has never been recognised by the United Nations.
Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, visiting Germany, denounced Ramos-Horta on Friday as a "political adventurist... repudiated by the majority of the people of East Timor".
"We do hope there is a message (in this award)...to the Indonesian government to change its policy," committee chairman Francis Sejersted told reporters at the Nobel Institute.
Congratulations for the winners came from Portugal, the Vatican, Australia, the European Union and the United States.
The U.S. State Department said it hoped the award would promote peace in East Timor but concern about human rights abuses would not affect plans to sell fighter planes to Jakarta.
Indonesian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl said said in Jakarta: "It is quite regrettable that such a reputable institution has decided to give this prize to a person like Ramos-Horta."
At least seven of the past 25 awards have caused a major stir.
Burmese opposition leader Aung San Kyi, the 1991 laureate, remained under house arrest in Rangoon until last year.
But the award gave her name a cachet which still helps to keep her, and the struggle of her democracy movement against Burma's military rulers, in headlines around the world.
The Dalai Lama, Tibet's spiritual and political leader, received the award in 1989 much to the chagrin of China.
During the Cold War, the Soviet Union and its East Bloc allies generally barred dissidents chosen for the Peace Prize from travelling to Oslo to collect it.
The late Andrei Sakharov, father of the Soviet nuclear bomb and peace prize winner as a dissident in 1975, was banished to a provincial city in 1979. He said the prize protected him from worse.
Lech Walesa, who won in 1983 when he was an anti-communist dissident and later became the post-communism president of Poland, also said the prize helped his cause and protected him personally.
Sejersted said it was the committee's role to take a stand on political affairs and turn the world spotlight on issues.
"This is fundamentally a political prize so that is what the whole thing is about," he said.
